newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Fresh talks aim to avert S.African trucking strike.
newsitem.headline: Fresh talks aim to avert S.African trucking strike.

text.p: Union and employer representatives in the trucking industry were set to meet on Monday afternoon in a renewed bid to avert a national strike over wages, a union official said on Monday.

Transport and General Workers' Union (TGWU) national organiser Thulani Dlamini told a news briefing the union had reviewed its original demand of a 14 to 18 percent across-the-board increase to 12.5 percent.
"We tabled a final show stopper offer this morning, dropping our demand to 12.5 percent across-the-board without which we cannot settle," Dlamini told reporters.
Employers subsequently acknowlewdged the revised position and requested a meeting for 1400 GMT on Monday, he said.
More than 83 percent of the members of the seven unions organised in the sector voted in favour of industrial action last week after a ballot.
Dlamini said the union had served employers the required 48-hour notice early on Monday, advising that a national strike would start on Wednesday.
"We are looking at a full-blown strike supplemented by pickets and marches," Dlamini said.
Employers are represented by the Road Freight Association.

Should the strike go ahead, it would spread across different sectors of the economy affecting the banking sector, air freight, waste companies, livestock vehicles, and the ferrying of chemicals and fuels.

Seven unions are organised in the industry, including the TGWU, the Professional Transport Workers' Union, African Miners and Allied Workers, the Turning Wheel Workers' Union, the Motor Transport Workers' Union, the South African Transport Workers' Union and the Transport and Allied Workers' Union.
The average wage in the industry is 321 rand per week for general workers in the bigger centres.
The union originally asked for a 14 to 18 percent across-the-board wage increase before revising on Monday.
Employers' last week raised their offer to ten percent after originally offering nine percent in late September when wage talks deadlocked.
